title: How to Improve Indoor Air Quality at Home
h1: How Can You Improve the Indoor Air Quality in Your Home?
description: Cleaner indoor air comes down to removing pollution sources, filtering well, ventilating and controlling humidity. Here are practical steps for any home.
quick_answer: Work on four things: remove the sources of pollution, filter the air, bring in fresh air, and keep humidity in check. In practice that means a good HVAC filter changed on schedule, clean ducts and coils, kitchen and bath fans that actually vent outside, and a purifier or dehumidifier where your home needs one.
body:
The air inside a house collects dust, pet dander, cooking fumes and moisture that have nowhere to go unless something moves them out. You don't need to overhaul your home to fix that. A handful of habits and a well-maintained HVAC system do most of the work.

What makes indoor air quality worse?

Indoor air picks up pollutants from everyday living. The common ones:

  • Dust and pet dander that settle and get stirred back up
  • Pollen that drifts in through doors and windows
  • Cooking smoke and grease, especially from gas stoves
  • Moisture from showers, cooking and coastal air, which feeds mold and dust mites
  • Chemicals from cleaning products, paint, new furniture and air fresheners
  • Wildfire smoke during Santa Ana season
  • Attic and garage air pulled in through leaky return ducts

That last one surprises people. In many San Diego and Orange County homes, the furnace and ducts sit in the attic or garage. A loose return connection can pull insulation dust, car exhaust or rodent debris straight into the system.

What's the easiest place to start?

The air filter. It's cheap, it takes two minutes to change, and it's the main thing standing between your ducts and your lungs.

  1. Find your filter, usually at a return grille in a hallway or ceiling, or in a slot at the furnace.
  2. Check the size printed on the frame and buy a pleated filter in a MERV 8 to MERV 13 range, depending on what your system can handle.
  3. Replace it every one to three months. Homes with pets, allergies or smoke may need it monthly.

A filter that's too dense for the system can choke airflow, so if you're jumping to a higher rating, ask a technician to check your system first.

How do you reduce pollutants at the source?

  • Use the range hood every time you cook, and make sure it vents outside instead of just recirculating.
  • Run bathroom fans during showers and for 15 to 20 minutes after.
  • Vacuum weekly with a HEPA vacuum and use doormats at every entry.
  • Store paint, solvents and pool chemicals in the garage, sealed, and away from the furnace.
  • Skip plug-in air fresheners and scented candles, which add chemicals to the air.
  • Don't idle the car in an attached garage.

Should you bring in more fresh air?

Yes, when the outdoor air is good. Opening windows on mild days flushes out stale air and odors. Our climate makes this easy for much of the year, and even 10 or 15 minutes with windows open on opposite sides of the house makes a difference. Skip it on high pollen days, during smoke events, and on windy Santa Ana days.

Newer, tighter homes may benefit from mechanical ventilation, which brings in a steady amount of filtered outside air without opening windows.

Do purifiers, UV lights and humidity control help?

They can, when they solve a real problem in your home:

  • Portable HEPA purifiers help in bedrooms and living areas, especially for allergies and smoke.
  • Whole-home air cleaners mounted at the furnace filter all the air the system moves.
  • UV lights at the coil help keep mold and bacteria from growing on wet surfaces.
  • Dehumidifiers help in damp coastal homes, and humidifiers help in dry inland homes during Santa Anas.

Avoid devices that produce ozone. Ozone is a lung irritant, even when it's marketed as purifying.

When should you have your ducts and system cleaned?

If you see dust blowing from vents, smell mustiness when the system runs, or recently had a remodel, rodents or smoke damage, it's worth having the ducts inspected. A dirty evaporator coil or blower can also put dust and odors back into the air. Annual HVAC maintenance catches these issues before they turn into air quality problems, and duct cleaning takes care of what has built up inside the ductwork.
faqs: What is the fastest way to improve indoor air quality?
Change your HVAC filter, open windows for a while if outdoor air is good, and run kitchen and bath fans. Those three steps make a noticeable difference the same day.

What humidity level is best for a home?
Roughly 30 to 50 percent is comfortable for most people and limits mold and dust mites. Coastal homes often run high, while inland homes can get very dry during Santa Ana winds.
How do I know if my indoor air quality is bad?

Common clues include dust that builds up quickly, musty or stale smells, condensation on windows, and allergy symptoms that improve when you leave home. An inexpensive air quality monitor can track particles, humidity and CO2.
